newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus rebuffs U.S. over criticism of missiles.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus rebuffs U.S. over criticism of missiles.

text.p: Cyprus on Tuesday rejected U.S. criticism of its purchase of Russian anti-aircraft missiles and said the system was essential to defend Greek Cypriots on the divided island.
"There is no issue of cancelling the agreement," Cypriot government spokesman Yiannakis Cassoulides told reporters.

"The Cyprus Republic needs to protect its people and has proceeded with an agreement with a country willing to sell us the system at advantageous prices," Cassoulides said, without giving further details.
The United States sharply criticised Cyprus on Monday for agreeing to buy the Russian missiles, saying it would introduce a new and destabilising element and undermine peace moves.
"This criticism is totally unfair," Cassoulides told Reuters.

"Similar criticism has never been raised against the presence of 35,000 Turkish troops illegally in Cyprus who are armed with American weapons...NATO weapons destined to be used against NATO enemies," he said.

Turkey has occupied northern Cyprus since an invasion in 1974 in response to a short-lived coup engineered by the military ruling Greece. The island's division remains a source of tension between NATO partners Greece and Turkey.

Purchase of Russia's S-300 system, with a 90-mile (145-km) range, is the Cypriot government's first step toward building a credible air defence system. The contract was concluded last weekend but it was unclear when the missiles would be delivered.
Government officials say the missiles will be deployed only for defensive purposes. They have not disclosed how many Cyprus is buying.
Turkey said on Monday it would not "tolerate" any change in the balance of power as a result of the decision to buy the missiles.
The United States also criticised Russia for selling the missiles to Cyprus. This was rejected by Moscow which said the sale did not change the balance of forces on the island.
United Nations' resolutions on Cyprus have called on both sides to cut their military spending.
Greek Cypriot military analyst Aristos Aristotelous said the deployment of the missiles would not alter the military balance on the island drastically.
"It creates obstacles to Turkish airplanes and while they are now 100 percent in control (of airspace over the island) this creates some challenges," he said.
Aristotelous, who heads the privately run Centre for Strategic Studies, said military spending in 1996 was at its lowest level in eight years.
"Military spending was 4.3 percent of GDP (gross domestic product) in 1996 from 6.5 percent in 1993 and seven percent in 1992," he said.
He said spending would reach four percent of GDP in 1997.
"Some claim there has been heavy purchasing by the national guard but this is not true," Aristotelous said. "In four years the government bought 41 T-80 U tanks from Russia and some carriers."

Tension along the U.N.-patrolled buffer zone dividing the island's two communities is at its highest for years, following the killing of four Greek Cypriots and one Turkish Cypriot in the area since last June.
